Earthquakes deepen inland as the slab descends, so the trench, the arc and the deepening earthquakes are the geological features of this convergent boundary. At boundary Y the plates slide horizontally past each other along a single fault. Friction makes the rock stick and then slip, releasing energy as shallow earthquakes. Each slip is felt as a shallow earthquake, and repeated movement gradually increases the offset along the fault. The rock on either side moves in opposite horizontal directions. Because no crust is created or destroyed and no volcanoes are present, the main geological feature is the fault itself.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses the subduction process at X and the stick-slip sliding at Y, linking each process to its features, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Boundary X is convergent, with the plate sinking and a volcanic arc forming on land. Boundary Y is a transform boundary, with shallow earthquakes along the fault but no volcanoes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes both processes with a feature for each, but the links are brief, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Boundary X has a trench and boundary Y has earthquakes along a fault.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a relevant feature at each boundary without describing a process, which meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a practical investigation to model normal faults, reverse faults and strike-slip faults

prompts.question: Outline how the student's sand model represents a normal fault, and what the downward movement of one block shows.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student builds a model using layers of coloured sand in a box. A sheet of paper set at an angle divides the box into two halves. The student pulls the two halves apart, so the upper block drops down relative to the lower block along the paper.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines how the pulled-apart sand layers and the paper represent a normal fault, and what the downward movement of the upper block shows
2 marks: Outlines the pulling apart of the model and links it to a normal fault
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the model
markerNotes: Map each part of the model to a feature of the fault, such as the paper as the fault plane.
Say which block moves and in what direction, since a normal fault has the upper block dropping down.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the upper block moves up, which describes a reverse fault rather than a normal fault.
Describing the sand moving without naming the fault type the model represents.

sampleAnswers.answer: The sand layers represent rock layers, and the sheet of paper represents the fault plane. Pulling the two halves apart represents tension, so the upper block drops down relative to the lower block along the paper, which is the movement of a normal fault. The model therefore shows that stretching of the crust produces a normal fault.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Maps the sand and paper to the rock and fault plane and describes the downward movement, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The paper is the fault and the sand layers move apart, so the upper block drops down as a normal fault.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the pulling apart and links it to a normal fault, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The sand shows layers moving in the model.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information about the model without linking it to a fault, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Assess how well a sand model represents a reverse fault and a strike-slip fault in the real Earth.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student uses one small box of dry sand to model a reverse fault by pushing the two halves together, and a strike-slip fault by sliding one half sideways past the other. The model is viewed from above only.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the model's validity for both reverse and strike-slip movement, identifies at least two limitations such as brittle sand and small scale, and makes a sustained judgement about what the model can show
5 marks: Assesses the model's validity for both fault types and identifies one or two limitations
4 marks: Assesses the model's movements and identifies one limitation
3 marks: Describes how the model represents one fault type
2 marks: Identifies a relevant feature of the model
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Assess both fault types, then judge what the model can and cannot show about real faults.
Name at least one limitation tied to the scenario, such as dry sand being brittle or the small scale of the box.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the model without judging how well it represents real faults.
Claiming the model shows the behaviour of faults at depth, which a small surface-viewed sand model cannot do.

sampleAnswers.answer: The model is a reasonable simplified representation of both fault types. Pushing the two halves together produces a hanging wall that rides up over the footwall along a thrust, which matches a reverse fault at a convergent boundary. Sliding one half sideways reproduces the horizontal movement of a strike-slip fault. However, dry sand is brittle and does not behave like deeper rock, which flows and bends under pressure, so the model cannot show how fault behaviour changes with depth. The box is also small, so the model cannot show the length or scale of real fault zones or the size of the earthquakes they produce. Viewing from above hides the three-dimensional shape of the fault planes. Overall, the model is valid for showing the direction of movement but not for predicting the depth or scale of real faults.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Assesses both fault types and gives several limitations, with a sustained judgement at the end, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The model reproduces the upward movement of a reverse fault and the sideways movement of a strike-slip fault. However, dry sand does not behave like deeper rock, so the model is limited.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Assesses the movements and names one limitation, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The model shows a reverse fault where the sand is pushed together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a relevant feature of the model without assessing it, which meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Use force diagrams to account for the presence of normal faults at divergent boundaries, reverse thrust faults at convergent boundaries, and strike-slip faults at transform boundaries

prompts.question: Classify the type of force shown by each of the three diagrams, and name the fault each force would produce.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student draws three force diagrams. The first has two arrows pulling the rock on either side of a fault away from each other. The second has two arrows pushing the rock on either side towards each other. The third has two horizontal arrows on either side of a fault pointing in opposite directions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Classifies all three diagrams as tensional, compressional and shear, and matches each with its fault type and plate boundary
3 marks: Classifies all three diagrams and matches two of them with a fault type
2 marks: Classifies two of the diagrams correctly
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Classify each diagram by the direction of its forces, then match it to the fault it produces.
Name the fault and the boundary type for each diagram, not just the force.
commonStudentErrors: Calling the pulling-apart force compression, which reverses the normal and reverse fault pairing.
Classifying the shear diagram as tension because its arrows point in opposite directions.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first diagram shows tensional forces, which pull the rock apart and produce a normal fault at a divergent boundary. The second diagram shows compressional forces, which push the rock together and produce a reverse fault at a convergent boundary. The third diagram shows shear forces acting in opposite horizontal directions, which produce a strike-slip fault at a transform boundary. Each force diagram therefore matches one type of stress with one type of fault and one type of plate boundary.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies all three diagrams and matches each with its fault and boundary, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first is tensional and the second is compressional, which give normal and reverse faults.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies two diagrams correctly without matching the third, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first diagram shows a force pulling the rock apart.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives relevant information from one diagram without classifying it fully, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Account for the presence of the thrust fault in the scenario, using the force arrows shown in the diagram.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A force diagram of a convergent region shows two large horizontal arrows on the continental crust on either side, both pointing inwards towards the middle. The diagram also shows a thrust fault in which the upper block is pushed up and over the lower block. Mapping of the rocks shows that they have been shortened horizontally.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Accounts for the thrust fault by linking the inward compressional arrows to horizontal shortening and to the upper block moving up over the lower block, and places it at a convergent boundary
4 marks: Accounts for the thrust fault by linking the compressional arrows to the upward movement of the upper block
3 marks: Links the inward arrows to compression and describes the thrust fault
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the force diagram
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Account for the fault by linking the force arrows to the movement, then to the shortening in the mapped rocks.
The thrust fault is the mechanism that takes up the shortening, so say so rather than only naming the fault.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the arrows without explaining how they produce the thrust fault.
Saying the upper block drops down, which describes a normal fault rather than a thrust.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the force diagram, the inward-pointing horizontal arrows show compressional forces pushing the continental crust together from both sides. When folding alone cannot take up this compression, the rock fractures along a low-angle plane. The upper block is then pushed up and over the lower block along the thrust fault, which shortens the crust horizontally and thickens it. Because the fault plane is inclined, the upper block rides over the lower block rather than sliding straight along the surface. This accounts for the horizontal shortening recorded by the mapping, because the thrust fault takes up that shortening. A reverse thrust fault of this kind is expected at a convergent boundary, where plates are pushed together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Links the inward arrows to compression, the upward movement on the thrust and the shortening in the rocks, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The inward arrows show compression, pushing the rock together, which causes the upper block to ride up along the thrust fault.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Links the arrows to compression and describes the thrust fault, which meets the 3-mark row but does not account for the shortening.

sampleAnswers.answer: The arrows show a force pushing the rock.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives relevant information from the diagram without accounting for the fault, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Construct annotated cross-section diagrams to account for the presence of mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys and the nature of volcanic and earthquake activity at ocean–ocean and continental–continental divergent boundaries

prompts.question: Identify TWO features that should be labelled on an annotated cross-section of an ocean-ocean divergent boundary.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is drawing an annotated cross-section of an ocean basin that is spreading apart. The section cuts through the centre of the basin, where the plates separate.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Identifies two features of the cross-section, the mid-ocean ridge with its rift valley and the shallow earthquakes or volcanic activity, and links them to plates separating
3 marks: Identifies two features of the cross-section and links one of them to plates separating
2 marks: Identifies one relevant feature of the cross-section
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name features that belong at an ocean-ocean divergent boundary, such as the ridge and its rift valley.
Link each labelled feature to the plates separating, so the annotation explains the feature rather than only naming it.
commonStudentErrors: Labelling a trench on an ocean-ocean divergent boundary, which belongs to convergent settings.
Labelling a ridge without saying that it forms where new oceanic crust is created.

sampleAnswers.answer: The annotated cross-section should label the mid-ocean ridge at the centre of the basin, where new basaltic crust forms and rises to a raised ridge. It should label the rift valley along the crest, where the plates are pulling apart and the crust is thinnest. It should also mark shallow earthquakes beneath the ridge and volcanic activity erupting along the crest, both caused by the plates separating. Together these labels show the features of an ocean-ocean divergent boundary.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names two features, the ridge with its rift valley and the earthquakes and volcanic activity, and links them to separating plates, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The cross-section should label a mid-ocean ridge at the centre of the basin, where new crust forms.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one relevant feature and links it to new crust, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The diagram should show the ocean and a ridge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives relevant information without identifying a labelled feature with a link, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Construct a written, annotated cross-section account of the continental divergent boundary in the scenario, labelling the rift valley, the normal faults, the volcanic activity and the shallow earthquakes.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A geologist describes a continent being pulled apart. The land surface is a long, low valley bordered by two steeply dipping normal faults. The valley floor has basalt lava flows and small volcanic cones, and shallow earthquakes cluster along both faults.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs an annotated account that labels the rift valley, both normal faults and the hanging wall movement, the volcanic activity and the shallow earthquakes, and explains how crustal stretching produces each
5 marks: Constructs an annotated account that labels most of the rift valley features and links at least two of them to stretching of the crust
4 marks: Labels the rift valley and its normal faults and links them to stretching of the crust
3 marks: Labels two or three relevant features of the continental divergent boundary
2 marks: Identifies one relevant feature of the rift valley
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Construct the account as a labelled description: name each feature, then explain it through crustal stretching.
Use hanging wall and footwall correctly, since on a normal fault the upper block drops down.
commonStudentErrors: Labelling the rift valley floor as rising, when the central block drops between the normal faults.
Listing the volcanic and earthquake features without explaining the stretching that causes them.

sampleAnswers.answer: The cross-section shows continental crust being stretched and thinned, so the land surface drops along two steeply dipping normal faults and forms a rift valley between them. The upper side of each fault, the hanging wall, is annotated as moving down relative to the footwall. The valley floor is annotated with basalt lava flows and small volcanic cones, which form where magma rises through the thinned crust as the plates separate; this volcanic activity marks the divergent boundary. Shallow earthquakes cluster along both faults and show where the crust is breaking under tension. Beneath the valley, the rising hot mantle is labelled as the source of the magma, and the crust is thinner here than in the adjoining continent. The annotations together explain how the continental divergent boundary forms.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Labels the rift valley, both faults and the volcanic and earthquake features, and explains each through stretching, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The valley is bounded by normal faults, which form as the crust is stretched and the floor drops. Lava flows and volcanic cones sit on the valley floor, and shallow earthquakes occur along the faults.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Labels the rift valley and faults and links the faults to stretching, which meets the 4-mark row. The volcanic and earthquake features are named but not explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: The land drops between two faults, forming a valley.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one relevant feature of the rift valley, which meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Construct annotated cross-section diagrams to represent the formation of ocean trenches, volcanic arcs, volcanic island arcs and mountain ranges in ocean–continental, ocean–ocean and continental–continental convergent plate boundary settings

prompts.question: Demonstrate, using labelled features, how an ocean trench forms at an ocean-continental convergent boundary.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student sketches a cross-section of an oceanic plate meeting a continent. The sketch must label the subducting slab, the ocean trench and the volcanic arc on the continent.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Demonstrates how the sinking oceanic plate forms the trench and how water released from the slab melts the mantle to form a volcanic arc, using labelled features
3 marks: Demonstrates how the subducting plate forms the ocean trench, using at least one labelled feature
2 marks: Identifies a feature of the ocean trench or volcanic arc
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Demonstrate the mechanism with labels, such as the subducting slab bending at the trench.
Give a reason for the volcanic arc, such as water released from the slab, rather than only placing the arc on the map.
commonStudentErrors: Placing the volcanic arc on the seafloor beside the trench.
Drawing the trench without showing the oceanic plate sinking beneath the continent.

sampleAnswers.answer: An oceanic plate is denser than the continental plate beside it, so at a convergent boundary it bends down and sinks beneath the continent. The bend creates a deep ocean trench on the seafloor, where the subducting slab enters the mantle. Water released from the slab lowers the melting point of the mantle above it, and the magma that rises forms a volcanic arc on the continent, inland from the trench. The labelled cross-section therefore shows the trench on the seafloor and the arc on land, both produced by the same plate.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Demonstrates the bend and sinking that forms the trench and the water-driven melting that forms the arc, using labels, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The oceanic plate sinks, which forms a trench in the ocean next to the continent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a feature of the trench and gives a brief mechanism, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: There is a trench and a volcano arc on the map.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives relevant information without a mechanism, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Construct an annotated written account of how a mountain range forms at a continental-continental convergent boundary, naming the features at each stage.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Two continental plates converge over millions of years. Marine sediments deposited on the margins of each continent are squeezed between the two plates before the intervening ocean has closed.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs an annotated account of the stages of collision, naming the suture, thrust faults, folded layers and crustal root, and explaining how the crust thickens and rises
5 marks: Constructs an annotated account of the stages of collision and names most of its features
4 marks: Describes the collision and the folding or thrust faulting, with at least one feature named
3 marks: Describes one stage of the collision with a feature named
2 marks: Identifies one relevant feature of the collision
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Give the stages in order, with the features of each stage labelled, rather than a general description of mountains.
Explain why the crust thickens: neither continental plate sinks, so the crust is stacked and rises.
commonStudentErrors: Describing a subduction trench as the cause of a continental collision mountain range.
Describing the mountains without naming the features that form at each stage.

sampleAnswers.answer: First, at this convergent boundary, the two continental plates move towards each other and the ocean between them is consumed by subduction, so the margins of the continents meet at a suture. Second, the sediments on the margins are folded and pushed up along thrust faults, forming fold and thrust belts. Third, because neither continental plate is dense enough to subduct, the crust thickens as the blocks are stacked on each other. Finally, the thickened crust rises isostatically and erodes, producing a high mountain range with a deep crustal root beneath it. The rock that was once on the ocean floor is now uplifted, which is why marine fossils can be found high in some mountain ranges. Each stage is annotated with its features: the suture between the continents, the thrust faults, the folded layers and the crustal root that supports the range.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives the stages in order with their features, and explains the thickening and rising of the crust, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The continents move together and the sediments fold along thrust faults, which thickens the crust and forms mountains.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the collision and the faulting with a feature named, which meets the 4-mark row but does not give the stages in full.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two continents collide and the rock is folded into mountains.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one relevant feature of the collision, which meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Analyse the scientific evidence, models and theories contributing to the formation of the Earth’s geological features

prompts.question: Outline TWO pieces of evidence in the notes that support the idea that continents have moved apart over time.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's notes list observations used to support the idea that continents have moved apart. The notes include fossils of the same freshwater reptile found in South America and southern Africa, and magnetic stripes on the seafloor that mirror each other on either side of a mid-ocean ridge.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines two pieces of evidence, the matching fossils and the mirrored magnetic stripes, and explains how each supports continents or seafloor moving apart
3 marks: Outlines two pieces of evidence and links only one of them to continents moving apart
2 marks: Outlines one piece of evidence from the notes
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Outline each piece of evidence and then say what it shows, not only what it is.
Link the magnetic stripes to new seafloor forming at a ridge, rather than to the continents directly.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the magnetic stripes are caused by the continents, rather than by reversals of Earth's magnetic field.
Listing evidence without explaining how it supports the idea that continents have moved apart.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fossils of the same freshwater reptile, such as Mesosaurus, are found in South America and southern Africa, which are now separated by an ocean. This evidence suggests the continents were once joined, because a freshwater animal could not have crossed the ocean. Magnetic stripes on the seafloor mirror each other on either side of a mid-ocean ridge, recording reversals of Earth's magnetic field as new seafloor formed at the ridge and moved outward. This shows the seafloor, and the continents on it, have moved apart over time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines two pieces of evidence and explains how each supports the continents or seafloor moving apart, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fossils of the same reptile are found on continents now separated by an ocean, which suggests the continents were once joined.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines one piece of evidence and what it suggests, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The notes mention fossils and magnetic stripes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information without outlining or explaining evidence, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Evaluate the scientific evidence, models and theories that explain the formation of Earth's geological features, from continental drift to plate tectonics.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A science class is comparing the early idea of continental drift, the model of seafloor spreading and the modern theory of plate tectonics. Students have data on fossils, rock ages, magnetic stripes and earthquake distributions to use in their evaluation.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Evaluates the scientific evidence and models in a sustained way, weighing the strengths and limitations of continental drift, seafloor spreading and plate tectonics and making a supported judgement about which best explains the geological features
6 marks: Evaluates the evidence and models with an explicit strength and limitation for each, supporting a judgement with some integrated evidence
5 marks: Explains how continental drift and seafloor spreading contribute to plate tectonics, with some evidence
3-4 marks: Describes evidence or a model for the geological features with some link to plate movement
2 marks: Identifies a relevant piece of evidence or model
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Weigh the evidence for each model, then judge which best explains the features; a list of evidence reaches only the lower rows.
Give a limitation for each theory and say why it matters, such as the lack of a mechanism in continental drift.
Use the named evidence from the scenario, such as magnetic stripes and fossils, rather than general claims.
commonStudentErrors: Describing continental drift, seafloor spreading and plate tectonics one after another with no judgement.
Stating that plate tectonics is proven beyond doubt, with no limitation discussed.
Calling magnetic stripes a driving force, which confuses evidence with mechanism.

sampleAnswers.answer: Continental drift proposed that the continents have moved apart over time. It was supported by matching coastlines, such as South America and Africa, and by matching fossils and rock types on opposite sides of the oceans. It was a useful hypothesis, but it lacked a mechanism to explain how continents could move through oceanic crust, so many scientists did not accept it. Seafloor spreading supplied a mechanism: new oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and moves outward. The scientific evidence for this includes the ages of the seafloor, which increase with distance from the ridge, and the symmetrical magnetic stripes that record reversals of Earth's magnetic field. Plate tectonics combines these ideas into a model in which rigid lithospheric plates move over the mantle, and it explains the geological features by linking each boundary type to earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain ranges and trenches. Its strength is the consistency of many independent lines of evidence, including the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes along plate boundaries. Its limitations are that the relative importance of the forces driving plate motion, such as mantle convection and slab pull, is still studied, and that it cannot predict when individual earthquakes will occur. Overall, plate tectonics is the most strongly supported explanation of the geological features, because its predictions have been tested by independent scientific evidence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Weighs the strengths and limitations of each idea and makes a supported judgement that plate tectonics best explains the features, which meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Continental drift used matching coastlines and fossils as evidence but lacked a mechanism. Seafloor spreading explained how the continents move, with magnetic stripes showing new crust forming at ridges. Together these ideas support plate tectonics as an explanation of geological features.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how continental drift and seafloor spreading contribute to plate tectonics, with some evidence, which meets the 5-mark row but does not evaluate the strengths of each.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fossils and magnetic stripes are evidence that continents moved.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies relevant evidence without explaining or evaluating it, which meets the 2-mark row.

subTopics.name: Rocks, minerals and the rock cycle

dotPoints.description: Distinguish between rocks, minerals and ores

prompts.question: Define a mineral, a rock and an ore.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class is preparing a glossary for a unit on Australia's geological resources. Each student must give the definitions in their own words, with the key feature of each term.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Defines a mineral, a rock and an ore, giving the key feature that separates each from the others
2 marks: Defines two of the three terms accurately
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about one of the terms
markerNotes: Give the key feature of each term, such as naturally occurring for a mineral, rather than a vague description.
An ore is defined by its economic value as well as its composition, so include the idea of being worth mining.
commonStudentErrors: Calling an ore any mineral that contains a metal, with no reference to economic concentration.
Defining a rock as a single mineral, which mixes it up with a mineral.

sampleAnswers.answer: A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and an ordered crystal structure. A rock is a solid aggregate of one or more minerals, or of other natural material such as volcanic glass. An ore is a rock that contains a metal or mineral in a concentration high enough to be mined and processed economically.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines all three terms and gives the key feature of each, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A mineral is a naturally occurring solid with a set chemical makeup. An ore is a rock that contains enough metal to be mined.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines two of the three terms accurately, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: An ore is a kind of rock.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives partly correct information about one term without a key feature, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Distinguish between a rock, a mineral and an ore, using the samples in the scenario to illustrate each.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A geology student collects three samples from an outcrop in western New South Wales. Sample A is a granite made of several interlocking minerals, including quartz. Sample B is a single crystal of quartz. Sample C is a rock that contains galena, a lead-bearing mineral, in a concentration high enough that a mine could process it for lead.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Distinguishes a rock, a mineral and an ore using the samples, explaining the defining feature of each and the key difference between them
4 marks: Distinguishes all three samples by composition, with one difference explained
3 marks: Distinguishes two of the samples by composition or economic value
2 marks: Identifies a feature of one sample
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Match each sample to one term, then explain what makes it fit that term.
Use the economic concentration of the metal to separate an ore from an ordinary rock containing the same mineral.
commonStudentErrors: Calling sample B a rock because it is a solid piece of material.
Classing sample C as a mineral because it contains galena, without the economic concentration that makes it an ore.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sample A is a rock, because it is an aggregate of several interlocking minerals, including quartz, with no single defined composition. Sample B is a mineral, because it is a single naturally occurring crystal of quartz with a definite chemical composition. Sample C is an ore, because it is a rock that contains galena, a lead-bearing mineral, in a concentration high enough to be mined and processed for lead. The key difference is that a mineral is a single substance, a rock is a mixture, and an ore is a rock whose value depends on its economic concentration of metal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Matches each sample to its term, explains the defining feature of each and states the key difference, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sample A is a rock made of several minerals, while sample B is a single mineral, quartz.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Distinguishes two samples by composition, which meets the 3-mark row but does not reach the ore.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sample C contains lead.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives relevant information from the scenario without distinguishing the samples, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Relate plate boundary types to the occurrence of mafic and felsic magma types

prompts.question: Outline the plate boundary setting most associated with mafic magma, and the setting most associated with felsic magma.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A geology student is making a table of volcanic rocks found at different plate settings. The table lists basalt from an ocean ridge, basalt from a hot spot in the middle of a plate, rhyolite from a continental volcanic arc, and andesite from an island arc above an ocean trench.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines the plate boundary setting for mafic magma and for felsic magma, and explains the source of each magma
3 marks: Outlines the plate boundary setting for both magma types with little explanation
2 marks: Outlines the plate boundary setting for one magma type
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name the boundary type for each magma, then give the reason, such as mantle melting at an ocean ridge.
Mafic and felsic describe the silica and iron content of the magma, so link each term to its composition.
commonStudentErrors: Placing felsic magma at ocean ridges, where basalt is produced.
Naming a plate boundary without saying which magma type it is linked to.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mafic magma is most associated with divergent plate boundaries, where the mantle melts as it rises beneath ocean ridges, producing basalt. Felsic magma is most associated with convergent plate boundaries that involve continental crust, where melting of the continental rock produces rhyolite. Intermediate magma is typical of ocean-continent subduction, so felsic magma becomes more common as more continental crust is involved in the plate boundary. Mafic magma is also produced at hot spots, but these occur away from plate boundaries.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the setting for mafic and felsic magma and explains the source of each, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mafic magma forms at divergent boundaries, such as ocean ridges.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the setting for one magma type, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Basalt is found at ocean ridges.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives relevant information about one rock without outlining a magma setting, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse the rock data in the scenario to deduce the plate boundary setting that produced rock Y and rock Z.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has a table of four volcanic rocks from different settings. Rock W is basalt from an oceanic ridge. Rock X is basalt from a hot spot in the middle of a plate. Rock Y is andesite from an island arc above a subduction zone where both plates are oceanic. Rock Z is rhyolite from a continental arc above a subduction zone where the overriding plate is continental.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the composition and setting of both rocks to deduce the plate boundary for each, and explains how the presence of continental crust changes the magma type
5 marks: Analyses both rocks and deduces the plate boundary for each, with some reasoning about the magma
4 marks: Analyses both rocks and deduces the plate boundary for at least one, with some support
3 marks: Describes the setting of one rock and links it to a magma type
2 marks: Identifies a relevant feature of one rock
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Deduce each boundary from the rock's setting first, then check it against the composition of the rock.
The presence or absence of continental crust is the key reason the same subduction setting can produce different magma types.
commonStudentErrors: Assigning rock Y to an ocean ridge because it is a basalt-type rock, when it is andesite.
Stating that rock Z forms at a divergent boundary without citing the continental arc in the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rock Y is andesite from an island arc above a subduction zone between two oceanic plates. Andesite is intermediate in composition, which fits a magma formed when water released from the subducting slab melts the mantle wedge above it, so the plate boundary is an ocean-ocean convergent setting, not a divergent ridge. Rock Z is rhyolite from a continental arc, where the overriding plate is continental. Rhyolite is felsic, so the felsic magma that produces it forms when melting involves continental crust, which is rich in silica. Continental crust is also less dense than the mantle, so magma generated within it tends to be silica-rich. The plate boundary for rock Z is therefore an ocean-continent subduction zone. The difference between the two settings is the presence of continental crust, which controls whether the magma is intermediate or felsic.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the composition and setting of both rocks and explains how continental crust changes the magma type, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rock Y comes from an island arc above an ocean-ocean subduction zone, and rock Z comes from a continental arc above an ocean-continent subduction zone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Deduces the plate boundary for both rocks with limited support, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rock Y comes from a subduction zone, so it is andesite.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a relevant feature of one rock without deducing the boundary, which meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Compare the chemical composition of mafic and felsic minerals

prompts.question: Describe TWO chemical differences between mafic and felsic minerals, using the examples in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's table lists four minerals: olivine, pyroxene, quartz and potassium feldspar. Olivine and pyroxene are grouped as mafic minerals, and quartz and potassium feldspar are grouped as felsic minerals.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two chemical differences between mafic and felsic minerals, using examples from the scenario
2 marks: Describes one chemical difference between the two groups, with an example
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the minerals
markerNotes: Describe the difference in both directions, for example mafic minerals contain more iron and magnesium while felsic minerals contain more silica.
Use the named minerals from the scenario as examples rather than general statements.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that felsic minerals are lighter in colour, which is a physical property rather than a chemical difference.
Naming the minerals without stating which chemical elements differ between the groups.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mafic minerals such as olivine are rich in magnesium and iron and contain relatively little silica. Felsic minerals such as quartz contain much more silica. Felsic minerals are also richer in aluminium, potassium and sodium than mafic minerals.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two chemical differences using named examples from both groups, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mafic minerals such as olivine contain iron and magnesium, but felsic minerals contain more silica.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one chemical difference with an example, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Olivine is a mafic mineral.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives relevant information from the scenario without describing a chemical difference, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse the chemical composition of olivine and quartz to explain what it shows about the magma each mineral crystallises from.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares two mineral samples. Olivine is a mafic mineral that contains magnesium and iron with relatively little silica. Quartz is a felsic mineral that is almost pure silicon dioxide.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the composition of both minerals and explains what each reveals about the magma it crystallises from
4 marks: Analyses the composition of both minerals with a partial link to the magma
3 marks: Describes the composition of one or both minerals and makes a link to magma
2 marks: Identifies a compositional feature of one mineral
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Link each mineral's composition to the magma it forms from, since minerals crystallise from the elements available in the melt.
Compare the two minerals directly, showing how the silica content differs.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that olivine contains no silica, when it contains some, but less than quartz.
Describing the minerals without saying what their composition reveals about the magma.

sampleAnswers.answer: Olivine is a mafic mineral that contains magnesium and iron with relatively little silica, so it crystallises from a low-silica magma rich in iron and magnesium, such as basaltic magma. Quartz is a felsic mineral that is almost pure silicon dioxide, so it crystallises from a magma that is rich in silica, such as rhyolitic magma. The chemical difference therefore reveals the magma each mineral crystallises from, because minerals form from the elements that are available in the melt. The contrast between the two minerals shows how the silica content of the parent magma controls which minerals can form.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the composition of both minerals and explains what each reveals about its parent magma, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Olivine is a mafic mineral with less silica than quartz, so it forms from a magma with less silica.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the composition of one mineral and links it to a magma, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Quartz contains silica.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives relevant information about one mineral without a link to magma, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a practical investigation to identify mafic and felsic minerals by observing their physical properties using a dichotomous key

prompts.question: Identify whether the unknown mineral is mafic or felsic, and give the key steps that lead to your answer.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student uses this dichotomous key on an unknown mineral. Key: 1a. Dark-coloured: go to 2. 1b. Light-coloured: felsic mineral. 2a. Dense, with a glassy lustre: mafic mineral. 2b. Less dense: felsic mineral. The unknown mineral is dark-coloured, dense and has a glassy lustre.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Identifies the mineral as mafic and gives both key steps used, linking each step to a physical property
2 marks: Identifies the mineral as mafic and gives one key step or property
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the key or the mineral
markerNotes: Give the key steps in order, and say which property sends you down each branch.
State the classification at the end of the key path, not only the properties observed.
commonStudentErrors: Calling the mineral felsic because it is dense, which reverses the key's density step.
Giving the answer without the key steps that lead to it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The unknown mineral is mafic rather than felsic. The dichotomous key starts at step 1a, because the mineral is dark-coloured, so the student goes to step 2. Step 2a applies because the mineral is dense with a glassy lustre, which identifies a mafic mineral.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the mineral as mafic and gives both key steps with the property that leads to each, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mineral is mafic because it is dark and dense, which the key shows.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the mineral as mafic with one property, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mineral is dark and glassy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives relevant observations without identifying the mineral, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Apply the key to the second mineral in the scenario, showing each step, and classify it as mafic or felsic.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's second unknown mineral is pale and has a low density. The student uses the same dichotomous key: 1a. Dark-coloured: go to 2. 1b. Light-coloured: felsic mineral. 2a. Dense, with a glassy lustre: mafic mineral. 2b. Less dense: felsic mineral.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Applies the key step by step to the second mineral, classifies it as felsic and explains why the other branch does not apply
4 marks: Applies the key to the second mineral and classifies it correctly, with one step explained

sampleAnswers.answer: The student begins at step 1 of the dichotomous key, which separates the mineral by colour. The second mineral is pale, so it matches step 1b, which is light-coloured, and the key stops there with a felsic classification. Step 2 would only be needed for dark minerals, so it does not apply here. The low density also agrees with a felsic mineral, since felsic minerals contain more silica and less iron and magnesium than mafic minerals. Had the mineral been dark and dense with a glassy lustre, the key would have led to step 2a and a mafic classification instead. The second mineral is therefore felsic.

dotPoints.description: Explain the roles of pressure, heat, weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction, cementation, melting and solidification in the formation of regional and contact metamorphic rocks, clastic and non-clastic sedimentary rocks, and intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks in the rock cycle

prompts.question: Describe the roles of compaction and cementation in forming a clastic sedimentary rock.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student finds a sandstone in a cliff face, made of sand grains that came from the weathering of an older granite. The student wants to explain how the loose sand became a solid rock.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes the roles of compaction and cementation in binding the sediment into a clastic sedimentary rock, with the process of each explained
3 marks: Describes the roles of compaction and cementation with some explanation
2 marks: Describes one of the processes and its role
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Describe each process in the order it acts, then say what it does to the grains.
Name the material that cements the grains together, such as silica or calcite, to show understanding of cementation.
commonStudentErrors: Describing compaction as the grains being heated until they melt together.
Saying the sand became rock only because it was weathered, which describes an earlier step.

sampleAnswers.answer: Compaction squeezes the loose sand grains together as overlying layers add weight, reducing the pore space between them. Cementation follows as dissolved minerals, such as silica or calcite, precipitate in the pore spaces and bind the grains together. Together, compaction and cementation convert the deposited sediment into a clastic sedimentary rock such as sandstone, made of fragments from earlier weathering. The grains keep their original rounded shapes, which shows that the rock is built from earlier material rather than formed by precipitation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how each process binds the sediment and names the rock formed, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Compaction presses the sand grains together, which forms a solid rock.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one process and its role, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The sand is cemented into a rock.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives relevant information without describing the role of either process, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse how the shale in the scenario could be changed by heat from an intrusion and by regional pressure, and the rocks each process produces.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A layer of shale, a clastic sedimentary rock, lies beside a body of magma that has intruded from below. A separate layer of the same shale is buried deep in a mountain belt during a period of regional compression.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how heat and regional pressure each change the shale, naming the contact and regional rocks produced and explaining the role of foliation and scale
5 marks: Analyses both processes and names the rock each produces, with some explanation of the change
4 marks: Describes both processes and names a rock produced by each, with limited explanation
3 marks: Describes one process and the rock or change it produces
2 marks: Identifies one process that changes the shale
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Analyse the two processes separately, because contact and regional metamorphism differ in scale and in whether the rock becomes foliated.
Name the rock each process produces, such as hornfels from heat alone, and slate or schist from regional pressure.
commonStudentErrors: Saying that the shale melts next to the intrusion, when it is changed while staying solid.
Describing both processes as the same, without separating heat from pressure.

sampleAnswers.answer: The shale is a clastic sedimentary rock made of fine fragments, so its change depends on whether it is heated or squeezed. Next to the intrusion, heat from the magma raises the temperature of the shale without large-scale pressure, which recrystallises the clay minerals into a fine-grained, non-foliated rock such as hornfels. This is contact metamorphism, which produces a contact metamorphic rock in a narrow zone around the magma. In the mountain belt, regional compression and heat during mountain building act over a large area, aligning the platy minerals so that the rock becomes foliated and forms slate or schist, depending on how far the change goes. This is regional metamorphism, which produces a regional metamorphic rock. Both processes change the shale without fully melting it, and the difference lies in the scale of the heat and pressure and in whether the rock becomes foliated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the contact and regional changes separately, names the rock each produces and explains foliation and scale, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Heat from the intrusion changes the shale into hornfels in a narrow zone, while regional compression in the mountain belt produces foliated slate or schist over a large area.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes both processes and names a rock for each with limited explanation, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Heat from the magma changes the shale, which becomes a harder rock.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one process that changes the shale, which meets the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a practical investigation using keys to identify clastic and non-clastic sedimentary rocks, intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks, and regional and contact metamorphic rocks according to their physical properties

prompts.question: Identify whether the sample is a clastic or non-clastic sedimentary rock, using the key in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student uses this key on a rock sample: 1a. Contains visible rounded fragments of other rocks: clastic sedimentary rock. 1b. No visible fragments: go to 2. 2a. Fizzes in dilute acid: non-clastic sedimentary rock (such as limestone). 2b. Does not fizz: not classed as a sedimentary rock in this key. The sample is made of rounded, sand-sized grains cemented together and shows no fizz in dilute acid.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Identifies the sample as clastic using the key, linking the physical property that leads to the step, and contrasts it with non-clastic rocks
2 marks: Identifies the sample as clastic and links it to a visible property such as rounded fragments
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the sample or the key
markerNotes: Name the key step you used and the physical property that sent you down that branch.
Contrast the result with the non-clastic branch, since a chemical or biological rock would not contain rounded fragments.
commonStudentErrors: Calling the sample non-clastic because it is solid and cemented, when cementation also occurs in clastic rocks.
Using the fizz test on a clastic sample, which does not identify it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The sample is a clastic sedimentary rock. Using the key, step 1a applies because the rock contains visible rounded fragments, and the sand-sized grains show that it is made of fragments of earlier rocks. Based on its physical properties, the sample is clastic rather than non-clastic, since a non-clastic rock would not be built from rounded fragments.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the sample as clastic using the key and contrasts it with non-clastic rocks, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The key shows rounded fragments, so the rock is clastic.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the sample as clastic with a visible property, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The rock has grains in it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives relevant information about the sample without identifying it, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Justify why a key based on crystal size and texture is more reliable than a key based on colour alone for separating intrusive from extrusive igneous rocks.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Two students design keys to separate igneous rock samples. Student P's key uses colour only: dark samples are called basalt and light samples are called granite. Student Q's key uses crystal size and texture: coarse, visible crystals suggest an intrusive rock, while fine or glassy textures suggest an extrusive rock. One sample is dark with coarse crystals, and another is light with a fine texture.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies the crystal size and texture key by linking these properties to cooling rate, and shows with a specific example why colour alone misclassifies rocks
5 marks: Justifies the key by linking crystal size and texture to cooling rate, with some reasoning about colour
4 marks: Explains that crystal size and texture reflect cooling rate and separates intrusive from extrusive rocks, with limited justification
3 marks: Describes crystal size and texture and states why colour is less reliable
2 marks: Identifies one property used in a key
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Justify the key by linking each property to how fast the magma cooled, not just by listing the properties.
Use a specific example from the scenario to show where colour alone gives the wrong answer.
commonStudentErrors: Saying that colour is useless, when it is a weak guide rather than having no value.
Stating that coarse crystals mean an extrusive rock, which reverses the link to cooling.

sampleAnswers.answer: A key based on crystal size and texture is more reliable because these properties reflect how the rock cooled. Intrusive rocks cool slowly beneath the surface, so they have coarse, visible crystals, while extrusive rocks cool quickly at the surface, giving fine or glassy textures. Colour does not reliably indicate cooling history, because both dark and light rocks can be intrusive or extrusive. Student P's colour key would call a dark coarse intrusive rock a basalt, which is an extrusive rock, so the key misclassifies it. Student Q's key uses texture directly, so it separates the two groups correctly. Crystal size and texture are therefore a more reliable physical test for the intrusive and extrusive distinction. Because they are visible in a hand sample, students can apply the key without a microscope, which makes the physical test practical for classroom use.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Links crystal size and texture to cooling rate and gives a specific misclassification from colour, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Crystal size and texture show how fast the rock cooled, so they separate intrusive and extrusive rocks. Colour alone can be misleading, as a dark coarse rock can be intrusive.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the cooling link and the weakness of colour with limited justification, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Crystal size can help tell rocks apart.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one property that could be used in a key, which meets the 2-mark row.

commonStudentErrors: Naming the tectonic process without saying how it produced the deposit.

sampleAnswers.answer: A tectonic process was the stretching and faulting of the crust, which created fractures and a basin in which hydrothermal fluids could circulate. An environmental condition was the sedimentary basin itself, which trapped sediments and fluids and allowed metals to concentrate in layers, forming the ore deposit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines one tectonic process and one environmental condition and links each to the ore deposit, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The crust was faulted, which let hot fluids move through the rock and deposit metal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines one tectonic process with a link to the deposit, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The deposit is in a sedimentary basin.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives relevant information without outlining a process or condition, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse how tectonic processes and environmental conditions combined to form a lead-zinc-silver ore deposit in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is studying a lead-zinc-silver ore deposit in western New South Wales. The host rocks are folded and faulted sedimentary rocks, deposited in a basin that was later deformed. Hot, metal-bearing fluids moved along faults and were trapped where the rock chemistry changed, forming the ore body.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the tectonic processes and environmental conditions in sequence, explaining how each contributed to concentrating the lead, zinc and silver in the ore deposit
5 marks: Analyses at least three factors and links them to the formation of the ore deposit, with some explanation
4 marks: Analyses two factors and links them to the formation of the ore deposit, with limited explanation
3 marks: Describes one factor and links it to the ore deposit
2 marks: Identifies one process or condition in the formation of the ore deposit
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Analyse the sequence: basin formation, then deformation, then fluid movement, then the chemical trap.
Explain how the environmental condition concentrated the metals, not only that the ore is present.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the ore body without the tectonic processes that formed it.
Saying the faults created the metals, when the faults only allowed the fluids to move.

sampleAnswers.answer: The tectonic processes began when the crust was stretched, forming a sedimentary basin in which the host rocks were deposited. Later compression folded and faulted these rocks, creating fractures and permeable pathways. Hot, metal-bearing hydrothermal fluids then circulated along these faults. The environmental condition that concentrated the metals was a chemical change where the fluids met a different rock chemistry or cooled, so dissolved lead, zinc and silver precipitated as sulfide minerals. The lead-zinc-silver ore deposit therefore reflects three linked factors: the basin that stored the rocks, the faulting that let the fluids move, and the chemical trap that caused the metals to settle out. The fluids also had to be hot enough to carry dissolved metals in solution, and each factor was necessary, so the deposit forms only where all three coincide.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the tectonic sequence and the chemical trap in order and explains how each concentrated the metals, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Stretching formed a sedimentary basin, and later folding and faulting let hot fluids move through the rock and deposit lead, zinc and silver.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses two factors and links them to the ore deposit with limited explanation, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hot fluids moved along faults in the rock.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one process in the formation of the deposit, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Lithium is a critical mineral used in the batteries that store renewable energy, and Australia has significant lithium deposits. Rare earth elements are a critical mineral used in strong permanent magnets for wind turbines, and their deposits are found in several states. Cobalt is also used in batteries. prompts.question: Assess how well Australia's critical minerals, their deposit locations and reserves can support a renewable energy economy, using the source summary.

Lithium deposits are concentrated in one remote region, far from the main population centres and the electricity grid. Rare earth deposits occur at several locations. The source lists cobalt reserves as small compared with projected demand for batteries. The source does not cover recycling of batteries or magnets.

sampleAnswers.answer: The critical minerals are important for a renewable energy economy because lithium and cobalt are used in batteries that store energy from solar and wind, and rare earth elements are used in turbine magnets. Australia's lithium deposits are concentrated in one remote region, which makes producing and transporting the mineral costly and makes supply depend on developing infrastructure there. The rare earth deposits occur at several locations, which spreads the risk and makes supply more resilient than a single deposit. The cobalt reserves are small compared with projected demand, so cobalt may limit battery production unless more reserves are found or the minerals are recycled. Overall, the reserves and deposit locations support a renewable energy economy for lithium and rare earths in the short term, but cobalt is a constraint. The source does not address recycling, which would reduce the need for new reserves, so the assessment is limited.

prompts.question: Describe how a geological map, remote sensing and direct sampling are each used to explore for a mineral deposit.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: An exploration company is planning a search for a copper deposit in an area with limited road access. The company has existing geological maps, satellite images and a budget for drilling.

sampleAnswers.answer: A geological map shows the distribution of rock units, structures and faults, so it helps the explorer identify where a copper deposit is likely to occur. Remote sensing uses satellite or aerial images to detect rock types, altered zones and vegetation changes across areas with limited access, which narrows the search area. Direct sampling involves collecting rock, soil or drill core samples, which are analysed to confirm whether the mineral deposit contains economic grades. Together these methods explore for geological resources in stages, from broad mapping to confirmation.

prompts.question: Examine how geological maps, remote sensing and direct sampling work together to reduce the cost and risk of exploring a remote region.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: An exploration company is searching a remote region with limited road access for a gold deposit. Its budget allows only a small drilling campaign. The company has an older geological map, satellite images that show zones of altered rock, and a plan to take surface samples first.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Examines how the three methods are sequenced to reduce cost and risk, explaining how each stage narrows the search before the next
5 marks: Examines the three methods and explains how at least two of them reduce cost or risk
4 marks: Describes how at least two methods focus the search, with a link to cost or risk
3 marks: Describes one method and how it is used in the exploration
2 marks: Identifies a relevant method or feature of the exploration
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Examine the methods as a sequence, with each stage narrowing the area for the next.
Link each method to cost or risk, such as cheap broad surveys before costly drilling.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the three methods without explaining how they work together.
Saying that drilling is cheaper than remote sensing, which reverses the cost relationship.

sampleAnswers.answer: Remote sensing is used first because it covers the whole region at low cost, and the satellite images show zones of altered rock that point to where mineralisation may be present. The geological map then narrows the search by showing the rock units, structures and faults that host the deposit, so drilling can be concentrated where the rocks are favourable. Direct sampling comes next: surface samples are analysed to confirm whether the altered rock contains gold, which avoids drilling in barren areas. Each stage reduces risk, because a poor result at one step stops further spending. The cost is lower overall because the cheapest methods eliminate most of the region before the expensive drilling campaign begins. Without this sequence, the company would have to drill across the whole region, which would be far more expensive and carry a much greater risk of a barren result. Together the three methods focus the exploration budget on the places most likely to contain an economic deposit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Examines the sequence of the three methods and explains how each stage reduces cost and risk, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Remote sensing covers the region cheaply and shows altered rock, and the geological map narrows where the drilling should go.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two methods focusing the search with a link to cost, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Satellite images and a geological map are used in exploration.
